title: 'Something was taken from us': Taresh Bobby Ramroop's family speaks out on SIU decision
subtitle: The man fell to his death in North York last October, while police were on scene. His mother shared a moving statement on Family Day about their loss.
article: The mother of a man who fell to his death from a North York highrise while police were on scene has released a statement for Family Day .

Her remarks come after last week's decision from the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) to not lay charges against the police officers present last October for the death of her son, Taresh Bobby Ramroop.

"The police must be held accountable for their recklessness, escalation and keeping us from Bobby," the statement read from Debbie Indal, shared on Twitter by author and activist Desmond Cole and grassroots coalition, Jane Finch Action Against Poverty . "We need to stop sending them into situations they will only make worse."

According to an initial SIU press release , Toronto police were called to an apartment on Jane Street and Finch Avenue West on Oct. 13, 2022, where a man was reportedly throwing objects from a balcony. The SIU said three officers tried to negotiate with him, and were joined by another three officers from the Emergency Task Force, before Ramroop fell from the window in the course of negotiations.

"No family should feel the pain we're feeling," Indal's statement read, renewing the family's call to reallocate police resources to "create new responses that de-escalate and communicate with people in crisis."

An Afro-Indigenous woman, Regis Korchinski-Paquet , similarly fell to her death in May 2020 after Toronto police responded to a call about a family dispute. The officers involved in that case were also cleared by the SIU, sparking demands for a nonpolice emergency mental health response.

While a mobile crisis intervention team (MCIT) exists - a program that pairs a mental health nurse with a specially-trained police officer - it was not deployed in Ramroop's case. Toronto police Chief James Ramer previously told the Star via email that this was because Ramroop had barricaded himself inside a bedroom, requiring "a higher level of response ... given elevated risk of harm."

Joseph Martino, Director of the SIU, noted in his report that the officers assigned to speak with Ramroop were trained negotiators. "It appears they did what they could to appease (Ramroop) and cajole him to safety," he wrote.

Martino said strategies, like rappelling down the roof or storming the bedroom were considered but ruled out, claiming Ramroop was "erratic and possibly armed with a knife." The report also mentioned "arrangements were being made to have a forensic psychiatrist attend the scene," but Ramroop fell before this could happen.

Vanessa Persaud, Ramroop's sister, said her family is "absolutely devastated" by the SIU's decision to not lay charges. "But we were expecting it because the SIU work for the police, so at the end of the day they're gonna have their backs, not ours," she said, adding that if officers are attending homes with past police history, that should have "nothing to do with the current call they're dealing with."

"We released our statement on Family Day because we feel like something was taken from us," Persaud said about her brother, whose life was cut short just two weeks before his 33rd birthday. She shared how Ramroop would deliver UberEats orders on foot to financially support his mom, in addition to working as a FedEx carrier. "Sometimes she was short to pay her bills and he was always willing to go that extra mile."

Persaud, Indal and their family plan to carry forth Ramroop's passion for graphic art, by selling colourful designs from the brand he started called Finch Town. "We will honour Bobby's memory as a son, a brother, a nephew, a grandson, a friend, an artist, a singer, a dancer and a member of a neighbourhood that adored him," Indal's statement said.
